tour.title: Historic Istanbul: Hippodrome to the Golden Horn
tour.summary: Three thousand years of empires on foot, from the Roman Hippodrome to the spice docks of Eminönü.
tour.overviewText:
Welcome to Istanbul. You are standing in the oldest part of the city, on a peninsula that has been fought over, rebuilt and renamed for more than two and a half thousand years. The Greeks called it Byzantium. The Romans made it Constantinople, capital of the eastern empire. The Ottomans took it in 1453 and made it the seat of a caliphate. Three names, three empires, all layered on top of each other in the streets you are about to walk.

This walk covers about three kilometres and takes in fourteen stops, from the chariot racetrack of imperial Rome to the ferry docks where Asia begins. You will see an Egyptian obelisk that is three and a half thousand years old, a mosque built to outshine its neighbour, a cathedral that became a mosque and then a museum and then a mosque again, and an underground reservoir held up by columns stolen from older temples. You will also walk through a working neighbourhood, because the old city is not a museum. People live here, shop here and argue over tea here.

The whole route takes roughly three hours at an easy pace, or a full day if you go inside everything. Most of the walking is flat and on pedestrian ground, but there are cobbles and some gentle slopes near the palace. Wear comfortable shoes.

Before you set off, three practical points. First, the two great mosques on this route close to visitors during the five daily prayers, so if you arrive and find the doors shut, wait a few minutes or come back. Second, ticket prices in Türkiye change often, so treat any figure in this app as a guide and check at the gate. Third, the tap water is fine but the tea is better.

Headphones on. Walk slowly, look up, and let me tell you what you are looking at.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Flat, paved and pedestrian for almost the entire route, with cobbles and gentle slopes near the palace.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Early morning, around 9am, before the square fills and while the light is soft on the domes.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.

stops.name: Obelisk of Theodosius
stops.narration: Standing in the middle of what was once the Hippodrome, this obelisk is far older than Istanbul itself. It was carved from a single block of pink granite in Egypt around 1479 BC, for the pharaoh Thutmose the Third, and it stood for nearly two thousand years at the temple of Karnak. In 390 AD the Roman emperor Theodosius the First had it shipped down the Nile, across the Mediterranean, and hauled up onto this spot. The marble base beneath it tells the story. Look closely and you will see Theodosius sitting in the imperial box, watching the chariot races, with his family beside him and captives offering tribute. The obelisk originally stood about thirty metres tall. It broke during the journey, so what you see today is only the upper section, roughly twenty metres. Even so, it has been standing here for more than sixteen centuries, which makes it one of the oldest monuments in the city.
stops.entranceFeeNote: It stands in the open on Sultanahmet Square. No ticket, no gate, open at all hours.
stops.accessibility: Level paved ground, step free from the square. The reliefs on the base are low and hard to see from a wheelchair.
stops.insiderTip: Look at the four corners of the marble base. The scenes are different on each face, and the one on the north side shows the obelisk being winched upright.
stops.nextStopDirections: Stay on the square and walk roughly twenty metres further south, along the same line of monuments. The next stop is the bronze column, and you will see it slightly to your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Apaleutos25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Serpentine Column
stops.narration: This bronze column has one of the strangest stories in Istanbul. It began as a victory monument at Delphi in Greece, cast from the melted weapons of the Persian army after the Greeks defeated them at the battle of Plataea in 479 BC. Three serpents twisted together, their heads holding a golden tripod. The Roman emperor Constantine had it brought here in the fourth century to decorate his new capital. For a thousand years it stood in the Hippodrome, until the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204. The golden tripod disappeared. The serpent heads were broken off, and one of them survives today in the Istanbul Archaeological Museum, just up the hill. What remains is about five metres of twisted bronze, and the names of the Greek cities that fought at Plataea are still engraved on the coils. Look at the metal closely and you can still make out some of the letters.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open monument on the square. The surviving serpent head is in the Istanbul Archaeological Museum, which charges its own ticket.
stops.accessibility: Right beside the paved path with level access.
stops.insiderTip: The column is hollow and was once a fountain, with water spouting from the mouths of the three snakes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue south along the line of monuments for about thirty metres. The third stop, a tall column built from rough stone blocks, is directly ahead of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Apaleutos25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Obelisk of Constantine
stops.narration: This one is easy to walk past, and that is a shame, because its story is a warning. It stands about thirty two metres tall and looks like rough masonry, but it was once covered in shining gilded bronze. It was built in the tenth century, during the reign of Constantine the Seventh Porphyrogenitus, which is where it gets its name. The emperor sheathed it in bronze plates so it would catch the sun and glow above the racetrack. Then, in 1204, the knights of the Fourth Crusade arrived. They were supposed to be heading for the Holy Land. Instead they sacked Constantinople, and they stripped this monument bare. The bronze went to the mint to be melted into coins. Compare it with the Egyptian obelisk a few steps away. One survived because it was solid granite. The other was dressed in something valuable, and that is exactly why it was destroyed. Acrobats once climbed this column during festivals and performed on top of it.
stops.insiderTip: This is the southern end of the old racetrack. From here you can see how long the Hippodrome was, which is hard to judge from the middle.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn around and walk back north along the square, past the Egyptian obelisk and the bronze column, for about two hundred and fifty metres. Keep the Blue Mosque on your right. The German Fountain is at the far north end of the square, an ornate domed structure you cannot miss.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Apaleutos25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: German Fountain
stops.narration: This ornate fountain is the newest thing in the square, and it is a gift from an emperor to a sultan. In 1898 the German Kaiser Wilhelm the Second visited Istanbul and was received by Sultan Abdülhamid the Second. The visit went well, and to mark it the Kaiser commissioned this fountain. It was built in Germany, shipped here in pieces, and assembled on this spot in 1901. The design flatters both sides. The octagonal shape, the marble, and the neo-Byzantine style all echo the city's own Byzantine past, while the golden mosaics inside the dome carry the Kaiser's monogram. The inscription around the top reads Wilhelm the Second, German Emperor, to his friend and ally the Sultan. It is worth stepping inside the colonnade and looking up at the ceiling. Notice too where it stands. It was placed at the head of the Hippodrome, on the ceremonial axis where emperors had once entered the racetrack, which was a very deliberate piece of stagecraft.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open to walk around and inside the colonnade.
stops.accessibility: Steps up to the fountain platform on one side, ramped approach on the other.
stops.insiderTip: Step inside and look straight up: the ceiling mosaics are gold and almost nobody looks, with the sultan's calligraphic signature and the Kaiser's crowned W alternating around the dome. The fountain also stands on grim ground. This was the site of the Vakvak plane tree, from which rebellious soldiers hung senior officials in 1656, earning it the name Bloody Plane.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn right and walk about two hundred metres south east, along the side of the square. The Blue Mosque is the huge building with six minarets in front of you. Head for the main visitor entrance, which faces the square rather than the park.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: A.Savin, FAL, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Blue Mosque
stops.narration: Most people call it the Blue Mosque. Its real name is the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, and it was built by Sultan Ahmed the First, who came to the throne at thirteen and commissioned this at nineteen. He wanted a monument to rival Hagia Sophia, and he wanted it right in front of it. The architect, Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa, completed the work between 1609 and 1617. The nickname comes from the interior, where more than twenty thousand hand made tiles from Iznik cover the walls, mostly in blue and green. The building handles light beautifully. There are two hundred and sixty windows, and much of the stained glass was made in Venice. Look up as you go in and you will see the great central dome, twenty three and a half metres across, ringed by four half domes so the whole structure cascades downward. The six minarets caused a scandal at the time, because only the mosque in Mecca was supposed to have six. The sultan solved that by paying for a seventh in Mecca.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free for worshippers and visitors. No ticket and no booking. Ignore anyone at the door offering to sell you entry.
stops.openingHours: Open to visitors from about 08:30 until around dusk, but closed to tourists during each of the five daily prayers, roughly 60 to 90 minutes each time. On Fridays it is closed to visitors until about 14:30. Prayer times shift daily, so check the day's timetable.
stops.accessibility: Step free route through the visitor entrance with a ramp. Headscarves are provided at the door and shoes are removed, so bring socks.
stops.insiderTip: The visitor entrance is on the square side, not the park side. If a long queue has formed, walk around to the courtyard on the far side, which is usually quicker and where you must enter anyway.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the mosque by the courtyard and walk north east, away from the Hippodrome, for about three hundred metres. You are heading towards the tram tracks and Hagia Sophia. The bathhouse is a long low building with domes, on your left just before you reach the square in front of Hagia Sophia.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Pedro Szekely from Los Angeles, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ayasofya Haseki Hürrem Baths
stops.narration: This elegant building is a hamam, and it was commissioned by one of the most remarkable women in Ottoman history. Hürrem Sultan was a woman from what is now Ukraine, taken captive and brought to the imperial court. She became the legal wife of Suleiman the Magnificent, which broke centuries of convention, and she was known in Europe as Roxelana. She was also a serious patron, and in 1556 she hired the empire's greatest architect, Mimar Sinan, to build this bathhouse. Sinan chose the site deliberately. It stands on the old Baths of Zeuxippus, which had served this square since Roman times, so the new hamam stepped directly into a thousand year old tradition. Look at the plan. It is a single building split down the middle, one half for men and one half for women, an arrangement that let both use the same heated core at the same time. It is the only hamam Sinan designed that way. After decades in other uses it was restored and reopened, and you can still book a bath today.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Not a museum: a working luxury hammam priced in euros. Packages run 110 EUR for 45 minutes, 155 EUR for 60, 220 EUR for 80 and 300 EUR for 110 minutes, roughly 6,100 to 16,600 TL. The lira figure moves with the exchange rate, so verify with the operator.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 07:00 to 24:00 in summer and 08:00 to 22:00 in winter. Reservations are strongly advised, particularly for evening slots.
stops.accessibility: The exterior is fully visible from the pavement. The historic interior has uneven heated marble and is not step free.
stops.insiderTip: This is a working hamam, not a museum. If you book, ask for a traditional scrub and foam wash rather than a massage package.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk on another two hundred metres towards Hagia Sophia. Just before you reach it, turn left down the side street where you will see a small sign for Yerebatan. The entrance to the cistern is on your right after about fifty metres.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gryffindor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Basilica Cistern
stops.narration: Underneath this street lies the strangest space in Istanbul. The Basilica Cistern was built in 532, in the reign of the emperor Justinian, to hold the city's water supply. It is enormous. The chamber is about a hundred and forty metres long and sixty five metres wide, and it can hold eighty thousand cubic metres of water. Inside, three hundred and thirty six columns rise in twelve rows to support the brick vaults, and almost none of them were made for this building. They were recycled from older temples and monuments around the empire, which is why they do not match in style or in height. Two of them rest on blocks carved with the face of Medusa. One is sideways, one is upside down, and nobody is quite certain why. The likeliest explanation is that the builders were reusing a pagan image and turned it over to neutralise its power. The water arrived from a reservoir near the Black Sea, kilometres away, carried here by aqueducts. Walk to the far end, then look back.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign adult daytime ticket 1,950 TL, per an official Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality notice of 3 February 2026. Turkish citizens pay 450 TL. Evening sessions, 19:30 to 22:00, cost 3,000 TL. Under sevens free. Turkish museum prices change often, so verify before you travel.
stops.openingHours: Open daily. Daytime visits run roughly 09:00 to 18:30, with a separate evening session from 19:30 to 22:00. Queues peak between 10:00 and 15:00, and the ticket costs more at night.
stops.accessibility: A long staircase leads down and back up, with no lift. The walkway inside is flat but can be slippery and is often crowded.
stops.insiderTip: Book a timed slot online in high season. The queue without a ticket regularly runs to an hour, and the inside is far quieter in the first hour after opening.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back up to street level and turn right. Walk about two hundred metres along the tram line, and Hagia Sophia will be directly in front of you, a large pink building with a great dome and four minarets. Head for the visitor entrance on the square side.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hagia Sophia Mosque
stops.narration: Almost everything about this building is a record of some kind. Hagia Sophia was built in just five years, between 532 and 537, for the emperor Justinian, and its architects were not builders by trade. One was a mathematician and the other a physicist. What they produced is a dome thirty one metres across and fifty five metres high, pierced by windows all around its base, so that it appears to float on a ring of light. It was the largest cathedral in the world for nearly a thousand years. Ten thousand people worked on it, and Justinian had materials brought from all over the empire, including porphyry columns taken from the temple of Artemis at Ephesus. In 1453, when Mehmed the Second took the city, he converted it into a mosque within days. It served as a museum from 1935 and became a working mosque again in 2020. Look up at the dome, then notice the great medallions and the mihrab sharing space with Christian mosaics.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign visitors pay about 25 EUR for the upper-gallery route. The fee is set in euros, not lira, so the lira equivalent moves daily. Worshippers entering to pray are not charged. Children under eight enter free with a passport. Istanbul museum passes do not cover Hagia Sophia.
stops.openingHours: Open to tourists daily, generally 09:00 to 19:30, opening at 08:00 from April to September. Closed to visitors during all five daily prayers. On Fridays the closure is longest, roughly 12:00 to 14:30, for the weekly congregational prayer. Last entry is well before closing, so do not arrive late.
stops.accessibility: Step free entry at the visitor gate with some uneven historic flooring inside. The upper gallery is reached by a steep ramp and is not accessible to wheelchairs.
stops.insiderTip: The interior is brightest in the afternoon, when the sun comes through the south windows and the mosaics in the apse are at their best. Enter with shoulders and knees covered.
stops.nextStopDirections: With your back to Hagia Sophia, walk to the right and up the slope towards the large stone gate with the fountain in front of it. It is about two hundred metres, gently uphill. That gate is the entrance to Topkapı Palace.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Adli Wahid, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Topkapı Palace Museum
stops.narration: This gate is the beginning of a palace that ran an empire for four hundred years. Mehmed the Second started building Topkapı in 1459, a few years after he took Constantinople, and it remained the sultan's residence until the 1850s, when the court moved across the water to Dolmabahçe. It is not one building but a series of courtyards, each more private than the last, which is how Ottoman palaces were meant to work. The further in you were allowed, the higher your standing. The first courtyard was open to the public, and the second was where the empire was actually administered. The third held the treasury, the harem and the sacred relics, and the fourth was the sultan's private garden. Inside you can see the mantle and sword of the Prophet, the Spoonmaker's Diamond, and the Topkapı Dagger, made famous by a Hollywood film. Budget two or three hours if you go in. The harem needs a separate ticket, and it is worth the extra.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Combined ticket covering palace, Harem and Hagia Irene: 2,750 TL for foreign visitors. Bought separately the Harem is 1,050 TL, so the combined ticket is better value. Turkish citizens pay 500 TL and Turkish students 100 TL. These figures come from an independent visitor guide, not the ministry site, so treat them as a strong indication and verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Open daily except Tuesday, 09:00 to 18:00, with the ticket office closing at 17:00. Closed on the first day of Ramadan Bayram and on 1 January. Last entry to the Harem is earlier than the palace closing time.
stops.accessibility: The first and second courtyards are step free. The third and fourth courtyards and the harem involve steps and uneven cobbles, and the harem is not wheelchair accessible.
stops.insiderTip: Go straight to the treasury and the sacred relics first, then work backwards. The tour groups all start at the same end and the queue for the relics can reach forty minutes by mid morning.
stops.nextStopDirections: Do not go through the gate. Turn around and walk back downhill, then take the first narrow lane on your right, which runs along the palace wall. This is Soğukçeşme Street, and it begins about thirty metres along on your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Carlos Delgado, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Soğukçeşme Street
stops.narration: You are now in the most photographed street in this part of the city. Sogukcesme means cold fountain, and the name comes from a fountain that once stood here. In the nineteen eighties this was a run down lane on the slope below the palace walls. Then a conservation campaign, led by the Turing Association under a man named Celik Gulersoy, rebuilt the Ottoman houses one by one. Look at the upper floors leaning out over the pavement. That overhang was not decoration. It shaded the walkway below and let neighbours lean out and talk across the street, which is how Ottoman lanes were designed to work. Here is the honest detail, and it is worth knowing. The houses are actually reinforced concrete faced with timber, not original wood, so this is a careful reconstruction rather than a survival. Nine of them form a hotel now, each named after the shrub beside it. Jasmine House, Wisteria House, Honeysuckle House. Come early and you will have the whole lane to yourself.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public street. The cafes and the hotel are private businesses.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times. It is a residential lane, so keep noise down early and late.
stops.accessibility: Pedestrian only and mostly level, with cobbles and a gentle slope at the lower end.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the bottom of the street and turn round for the classic view, with the timber houses on both sides and the palace wall closing the top of the frame.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow the street down to the bottom and turn left along the main road. Walk about three hundred metres, passing the entrance to the archaeological museum on your right. The main gate of Gülhane Park is on your right, a short way past the museum.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gryffindor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gülhane Park
stops.narration: This is the oldest park in Istanbul, and it was once the private garden of the sultans. The name means rosehouse, after the rose gardens the palace kept here. The park is the outer garden of Topkapı, laid out on the slope that runs down to the water, and it was opened to the public in 1912. It matters politically as well as botanically. In 1839 a decree known as the Gülhane Hatt-ı Hümayun was read out here in the presence of the young sultan Abdülmecid. It promised security of life and property for all subjects, taxation by law, and an end to arbitrary execution, and it is usually treated as the starting point of the Tanzimat reforms. Walk north to the far end and you will find a much older monument: a Roman column known as the Goths' Column, which commemorates a victory over the Goths and has stood here for about seventeen centuries. It is one of the oldest surviving Roman monuments in the city, and almost everyone walks past it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free admission to the park. The Museum of the History of Science and Technology in Islam, inside the park, charges a separate modest ticket.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, broadly dawn until late evening, around 06:00 to 22:00 in summer with shorter hours in winter. Hours vary by season, so verify at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Main paths are wide and paved with gentle gradients. Some side paths and the area around the Goths' Column are steep and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: The tea garden at the northern end sits on the old palace walls with a view over the Bosphorus. It is cheap and it is the best view on the whole walk.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the park by the main gate and turn right along the tram line. Walk west for about three hundred and fifty metres, keeping the tram tracks on your left. Cross towards the small mosque and the lanes behind Sirkeci station. That cluster of streets is Hoca Paşa.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Maurice Flesier, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hoca Paşa
stops.narration: You have just crossed into a different neighbourhood, and a different mood. Hoca Paşa takes its name from a fifteenth century vizier who served Mehmed the Second, the sultan who conquered the city. The small mosque you can see nearby still carries his name, and it has been rebuilt several times after fires and earthquakes. What makes this area interesting is that it sits right behind Sirkeci railway station. From 1890 that station was the terminus of the Orient Express, the train that brought European travellers from Paris to the edge of the Ottoman world, and many of them stepped out into exactly these streets. The neighbourhood filled up with small hotels for them, and it still works that way today. It is also a good place to eat. The lanes around here are full of simple lokantas serving home style Turkish cooking at honest prices, well away from the photographed menus in the square you left behind.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public neighbourhood, no ticket. Expect to pay for food and drink only.
stops.openingHours: Always open. Lunchtime is the best moment, when the lokantas are full of local office workers.
stops.accessibility: Narrow pavements and some steep side streets. Main routes through are paved.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the handwritten menu taped in the window and a queue of men in shirtsleeves at midday. That is the test for a good lokanta around here.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north west for about five hundred metres, crossing the main road towards the water. You are heading for a large stone building with a row of domes along its roof. The spice bazaar entrance is on the far side, next to the mosque.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Martin Dürrschnabel, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Egyptian Bazaar
stops.narration: This is the Egyptian Bazaar, known in Turkish as Mısır Çarşısı, and it is the second great covered market of Istanbul after the Grand Bazaar. It was commissioned by Turhan Sultan, the mother of Sultan Mehmed the Fourth, and built between 1660 and 1664. She was a powerful figure who acted as regent for her young son, and the rents from these shops paid for the New Mosque next door, which is why the two buildings stand so close together. The bazaar is L shaped, with around eighty five shops, and it was the centre of the spice trade for the whole city. The name is usually explained by the spices that arrived here from Egypt, though it may also refer to a market in Cairo that this one was modelled on. You will find saffron, sumac, dried figs, Turkish delight, caviar, and mountains of tea, alongside herbs still sold for medicine. It is busy, so keep an eye on your bag and enjoy the smell.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay only for what you buy. Bargaining is expected, and opening prices are often a third to a half above what a seller will accept.
stops.openingHours: Open every day including Sunday, roughly 08:00 to 19:30 Monday to Saturday and from about 09:30 on Sundays. Closed on the main days of Ramadan Bayram and Kurban Bayram. Note that the Grand Bazaar, unlike this one, shuts all day Sunday.
stops.accessibility: Level entrance from the waterfront side and a paved floor. The lanes are narrow and very crowded, which is the main difficulty rather than steps.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the far end and use the exit by the New Mosque, then look back at the building from outside. The L shape and the domes make much more sense from there than from inside.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the waterfront exit and walk towards the water. The ferry terminals are directly ahead of you, about a hundred metres away, along with the bridges over the Golden Horn.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Robot8A, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Eminönü
stops.narration: You have reached the water, and this is where the walk ends. Eminönü is the historic landing place on the Golden Horn. The name comes from the Ottoman customs service based here, in front of which officials collected duty on everything entering the city by sea. The square beside you holds the New Mosque, begun in the fifteen nineties and finally completed in 1663, and its name is a reminder of how long these projects could take. The piers in front of you are among the busiest in Istanbul, with ferries crossing to Kadıköy and Üsküdar on the Asian side, and boats running up the Golden Horn and out along the Bosphorus. From this spot you have the old city on one side and the water, the bridges and the modern city on the other. If you have time, take a ferry. It is the cheapest sightseeing in Istanbul, and it gives you the skyline you have been walking through all day from exactly the right distance. Thank you for walking with me.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public waterfront, no ticket. Ferries, food and the Galati Bridge are pay-as-you-go. An Istanbulkart is the cheapest way onward.
stops.openingHours: Always open. Ferries run from early morning until around 11pm, most frequently at commuter hours.
stops.accessibility: Wide level promenade with step free access to the ferry piers, though boarding a moving ferry can be difficult for some visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Buy an Istanbulkart from the machines by the piers, then take the short crossing to Kadıköy. Sit on the right hand side going out for the best view of the old city skyline.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the final stop. The walk ends here at the waterfront, with the ferry piers in front of you and the Galata Bridge to your left. If you want to continue, the Spice Bazaar is behind you and the Galata Tower is across the bridge, about twenty minutes on foot.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jorge Láscar from Australia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
